abstract: Poorly differentiated lung adenocarcinoma (PDLA) is the most aggressive subtype and characterized by early metastasis, rapid progression, and a dismal prognosis. Glutathione peroxidase 8 (GPX8) is frequently upregulated in poorly differentiated tumors and closely associated with poor survival, yet its specific role in the invasion and metastasis of PDLA remains poorly defined. Emerging evidence implicates GPX8 in calcium (Ca²⁺) homeostasis; therefore, we investigated whether GPX8 promotes the invasion and metastasis of PDLA by regulating Ca²⁺ signaling. Bioinformatics analysis, immunohistochemistry (IHC), western blotting (WB), and next-generation sequencing (NGS) consistently confirmed high expression levels of GPX8 in PDLA tissues and NCI-H1975 cell lines. The overexpression of GPX8 depleted Ca²⁺ stores in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and enhanced Ca²⁺ influx in a manner that was partially dependent on Orai1-mediated store-operated calcium entry (SOCE) and could be attenuated by CM 4620 (dual Orai1/2 channel inhibitor)and knockdown of Orai1. The effect of SOCE induced by thapsigargin (TG) was analogous to the phenomenon observed upon GPX8 overexpression, and this classical SOCE-mediated Ca²⁺ influx was almost completely abrogated by treatment with 20 μM of CM4620 (P < 0.01). Moreover, GPX8 downregulated E-cadherin, upregulated Vimentin, promoted invasion in vitro, and induced lung metastasis in nude mice. Interestingly, siRNA-mediated Orai1 knockdown elevated E-cadherin expression, reduced Vimentin levels, and suppressed epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT). Bioinformatics prediction and dual-luciferase reporter assays verified that the Ca²⁺-dependent transcription factors CREB1 and CREB3 positively regulated GPX8 transcription, forming a potential feed-forward loop to amplify SOCE signaling. Our findings reveal that GPX8 acts as a critical driver of PDLA invasion and metastasis via CREB1/3-regulated SOCE-mediated Ca²⁺ signaling and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), suggesting that targeting the GPX8/SOCE/Ca²⁺ axis may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for PDLA.
